authoritative_sources.title: Albinism and genetics
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: AboutKidsHealth, The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids)
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The SickKids-hosted genetics page was checked directly and is used only for stable phenotype and inheritance recognition.

authoritative_sources.title: Genetic tests available
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The current Canadian laboratory catalogue was checked directly; it is used only to confirm the distinct inherited-condition diagnostic context, not to direct testing.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize inherited genodermatoses by their core phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa causes inherited skin fragility and trauma-induced blistering, while oculocutaneous albinism causes reduced pigment involving the eyes, skin, and hair; inherited ichthyosis belongs in the rare-genodermatosis differential rather than the acute blistering differential.

source_citations.locator: About the Clinic; three major EB types; genetically inherited disorders and blistering
Key points; What is albinism?; OCA usually has autosomal recessive inheritance
Skin, Bone & Immune System panel list: congenital ichthyosis, epidermolysis bullosa, and oculocutaneous albinism

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Do not treat congenital trauma-induced blistering as ordinary acquired friction injury; epidermolysis bullosa has distinct inherited subtypes and requires specialist care.

source_citations.locator: About the Clinic; What are the different types of EB?

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: Canadian paediatric specialty-centre and Canadian genetics-laboratory sources provide the needed stable recognition evidence; no international fallback is used.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports only recognition of the inherited phenotype and appropriate distinction from common acquired conditions; it does not specify genetic testing pathways, wound-care products, or treatment regimens.

evidence_notes: Rare-disease management and diagnostic testing are intentionally outside this diagnosis packet.

authoritative_sources.title: Vitiligo
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CDA current disease-information page was checked directly at retrieval.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize vitiligo as an autoimmune loss of melanocytes producing milky-white irregular patches, and assess for associated autoimmune disease rather than treating depigmentation as a purely cosmetic finding.

source_citations.locator: What is Vitiligo?; Signs & Symptoms; Causes

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Vitiligo is not contagious, and confirmation or autoimmune investigation should be individualized when the presentation is uncertain.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports clinical recognition and the autoimmune-association boundary only; it does not encode topical, phototherapy, JAK-inhibitor, or surgical treatment selection.

evidence_notes: Medication and procedure claims are excluded from this diagnosis-only packet.

authoritative_sources.title: Basal Cell Carcinoma
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CDA current disease-information page was checked directly at retrieval.

authoritative_sources.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CDA current disease-information page was checked directly at retrieval.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize basal cell carcinoma as a persistent pearly or pink lesion with a rolled border or surface telangiectasia, and squamous cell carcinoma as a thickened red scaly, wart-like, crusted, or nonhealing lesion; both warrant timely clinical assessment.

source_citations.locator: Appearance; What is Squamous Cell Carcinoma?

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A nonhealing sore or a changing lesion should not be reassured as benign solely because it is small or minimally symptomatic.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports lesion recognition and urgency only; it does not specify biopsy type, excision margin, staging, or treatment modality.

evidence_notes: Management details require current lesion- and jurisdiction-specific specialty care evidence.

authoritative_sources.title: Seborrheic Keratoses
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: HealthLink BC's current reviewed page is used for stable benign-lesion recognition and uncertainty boundaries, not treatment selection.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize seborrheic keratosis as a common benign, slowly growing waxy, rough, or bumpy lesion whose appearance can overlap with other skin growths; assess a rapidly changing, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesion rather than assuming a benign diagnosis.

source_citations.locator: What are seborrheic keratoses?; What are the symptoms?; Should you worry about seborrheic keratoses?

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Clinical appearance alone may not reliably distinguish a benign keratosis from a mole, wart, skin tag, or melanoma when a lesion is atypical.

source_citations.locator: What are the symptoms?; How are seborrheic keratoses diagnosed?

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The current Canadian provincial health-service source supplies the necessary stable benign-lesion recognition and referral boundary without an international fallback.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports recognition of common benign-growth patterns and diagnostic uncertainty only; it does not encode removal methods or any cancer-treatment decision.

source_citations.locator: How are seborrheic keratoses treated?; Should you worry about seborrheic keratoses?

evidence_notes: The broader benign-lesion list remains recognition-only because specific lesion morphology varies.

supported_recommendations.statement: Use the ABCDE features—asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter, and evolution—to recognize a suspicious pigmented lesion, particularly a changing lesion, and arrange prompt clinical assessment.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Melanoma can have variable colour and subtype-specific morphology; a concerning evolution should not be dismissed because a lesion does not fit a single stereotyped appearance.

authoritative_sources.title: Swollen Glands, Hernias, and Other Lumps Under the Skin
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The current Alberta public-health page was checked directly and is used only for stable clinical-description recognition.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize common benign subcutaneous lesions by pattern: a lipoma is typically a smooth, rubbery, mobile dome-shaped lump, whereas a cyst is a sac containing fluid or debris and may be tender.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A changing, painful, infected, fixed, or diagnostically uncertain lump needs clinical assessment rather than routine reassurance.

source_citations.locator: Swollen Glands, Hernias, and Other Lumps Under the Skin; Non-cancerous (benign) growths

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: A current Canadian provincial health-service source adequately supports stable recognition of common benign lumps without international fallback.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports recognition of typical benign cyst and lipoma patterns only; it does not determine imaging, biopsy, excision, or antimicrobial management.

evidence_notes: The packet does not infer malignancy exclusion from a single descriptive feature.

authoritative_sources.title: Swollen Glands, Hernias, and Other Lumps Under the Skin
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The current Alberta public-health page was checked directly and is used only for stable clinical-description recognition.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize a skin cyst as a sac containing fluid or debris that commonly occurs on the scalp, ears, face, or back; distinguish this superficial lesion pattern from a mobile lipoma or an acute inflammatory mass.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Tenderness or other concerning change in a cyst-like lesion should prompt assessment for a complication or an alternative diagnosis.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: A current Canadian provincial health-service source provides the required stable cyst-recognition evidence without international fallback.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports common superficial-cyst recognition only; it does not prescribe diagnostic imaging, drainage, excision, or pathology.

evidence_notes: Cyst subtype naming and procedures are excluded from this basic diagnosis packet.

authoritative_sources.title: 2021 Canadian Cardiovascular Society Guidelines for the Management of Dyslipidemia for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease in Adults
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CCS guideline resource was checked directly and is used for the stable association of xanthoma with dyslipidemia, not for treatment selection.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize a lipoma as a smooth, rubbery, mobile benign-appearing lump, and recognize xanthoma or xanthelasma as a physical stigma of dyslipidemia that warrants lipid-focused clinical assessment.

source_citations.locator: Stigmata of dyslipidemia: corneal arcus, xanthelasma or xanthoma

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A presumed lipoma that is atypical or diagnostically uncertain should not be managed as a routine benign lesion without assessment.

source_citations.locator: Swollen Glands, Hernias, and Other Lumps Under the Skin

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: A Canadian provincial health-service source and current Canadian cardiovascular specialty guideline collectively support recognition of lipoma and systemic interpretation of xanthoma without international fallback.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports lesion recognition and the dyslipidemia-association boundary only; it does not prescribe imaging, lesion removal, lipid thresholds, or lipid-lowering treatment.

evidence_notes: The packet deliberately does not turn xanthoma recognition into a treatment algorithm.

authoritative_sources.title: Alopecia
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CDA current disease-information page was checked directly at retrieval.

supported_recommendations.statement: Differentiate common alopecia patterns: androgenetic alopecia produces patterned frontal or crown thinning, alopecia areata produces random round patches, and scarring alopecia causes permanent follicle loss and requires dermatologic assessment.

source_citations.locator: Types of Hair Loss: Male pattern baldness; Female pattern baldness; Alopecia areata; Scarring alopecias

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Do not promise regrowth in scarring alopecia: follicles are replaced by scar tissue and the stated goal is to prevent progression.

source_citations.locator: Types of Hair Loss: Scarring alopecias

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports pattern recognition and referral significance only; it does not prescribe hormonal testing, scalp biopsy technique, or pharmacologic treatment.

source_citations.locator: Types of Hair Loss; Managing Hair Loss

evidence_notes: Hypertrichosis and hirsutism differentiation requires a separate endocrine-context packet if management is tested.

authoritative_sources.title: Vascular anomalies in childhood: When to treat and when to refer
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The current CPS practice point was checked directly and is used for stable vascular-anomaly terminology, natural history, and referral-risk recognition.

supported_recommendations.statement: Distinguish proliferative vascular tumours such as infantile hemangioma from vascular malformations; infantile hemangiomas typically grow in the first weeks to months after birth and then involute, while high-risk location, ulceration, functional compromise, or large segmental facial involvement warrants early specialist referral.

source_citations.locator: Background and prevalence; Infantile hemangiomas; When to treat and when to refer

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Congenital hemangioma is distinct from infantile hemangioma because it is fully developed at birth and does not show the early proliferative phase.

evidence_boundaries.statement: This packet supports terminology, natural-history recognition, and referral-risk identification only; it does not encode propranolol dosing, treatment initiation protocol, or malformation intervention selection.

source_citations.locator: Infantile hemangiomas; Other vascular anomalies; Key practice points

evidence_notes: Medication and intervention details are deliberately excluded despite the source discussing them.
